assumptions.name: Exponential Time Hypothesis
assumptions.definition: There is a positive exponential rate below which deterministic variable-3SAT cannot be solved.
assumptions.model: Deterministic decision on explicit 3-CNF formulas. Let n be the number of variables and L the complete input length.
assumptions.quantifiers: There exists δ > 0 such that, for every fixed C ≥ 0, no correct algorithm runs in O(2^(δ n) L^C).
assumptions.conventions: Variable-count positive-rate convention. Solvers at different rates in the negation may be different algorithms.

source.locator: Definition of s_k and Theorem 1, item 3, p. 368

assumptions.name: Satisfiability Hypothesis
assumptions.definition: The deterministic decision power index of CNF-SAT is one.
assumptions.model: Explicit CNF-SAT with the source encoding length as the size measure.
assumptions.quantifiers: For each fixed 0 < a < 1 there is no deterministic 2^O(n^a) · poly(n) SAT algorithm, with n the normalized input length.
assumptions.conventions: Whole fixed-power exclusion family. Conversions to variable count, clause count or combinatorial length require the stated normalization or sparsification argument.

source.locator: Definition 2.1, p. 210, and Satisfiability Hypothesis, §2, p. 213

assumptions.access: Stearns and Hunt introduced SH. For the normalized length convention, see the introduction and footnotes 1–2 in arXiv:2611.02650v2, pp. 1–2.

assumptions.name: FPT ≠ W[1]
assumptions.definition: Some parameterized problem in W[1] has no deterministic fixed-parameter tractable decision algorithm.
assumptions.model: Deterministic uniform algorithms on explicitly encoded inputs, under fixed-parameter reductions.
assumptions.quantifiers: An FPT algorithm has time f(k) · L^C for a computable function f, a fixed constant C, parameter k, and complete input length L.
assumptions.conventions: No restriction to polynomial, elementary or quasipolynomial growth of f. Randomized separation would be another premise.

assumptions.name: NP ⊈ QP
assumptions.definition: There is a language in NP outside deterministic quasipolynomial time.
assumptions.model: Deterministic worst-case decision time on complete binary inputs of length L.
assumptions.quantifiers: QP is the union over fixed c ≥ 1 of DTIME(2^O((log(L+2))^c)). Containment would allow a language-specific algorithm and exponent.
assumptions.conventions: The complete bit length controls the exponent. An arbitrary FPT factor in a parameter need not be quasipolynomial in L.
assumptions.access: Class-separation premise stated directly in terms of the defining time classes. No priority or originating-paper attribution is asserted.

assumptions.name: k × k Clique Hypothesis
assumptions.definition: Given an explicit k × k array of vertices and their edges, no deterministic 2^(o(k log₂ k))-time algorithm decides whether a clique meets every row.
assumptions.quantifiers: The exclusion concerns the worst-case running time as the number of rows k grows.
assumptions.conventions: The selected vertices may share columns.

source.locator: Section 2, hypothesis definition on p. 2 and deterministic convention on p. 3

proofs.title: Vertex-Disjoint Paths at optimal width on subcubic bipartite graphs

theorems.label: vdp-width-w1
theorems.statement: Under deterministic FPT ≠ W[1], there is no correct deterministic Vertex-Disjoint Paths solver in 2^{h(w)} B^C time for a fixed C and a finite nonnegative h effectively little-o of max(1, w log₂(max(2,w))). The parameter is intrinsic treewidth or the width of a supplied path decomposition. The hard instances are connected bipartite graphs of maximum degree three with distinct leaf demand endpoints and equal treewidth and pathwidth. The supplied path decomposition is optimal.

formulations.name: Uniform ETH
formulations.statement: No single deterministic algorithm decides 3-SAT in time 2^(o(n)) L^(O(1)), where n is the number of variables and L is the input length in bits.

equivalences.forward:
Suppose there were a single subexponential algorithm for 3-Coloring. For each fixed positive integer j, sparsification splits a 3-SAT instance on n variables into at most 2^(n/j) formulas. Each has linearly many clauses for fixed j and reduces to a graph with linearly many vertices. Running the coloring algorithm on these graphs decides 3-SAT in time 2^(n/j+o(n)), up to a polynomial input factor.

To obtain a single 3-SAT algorithm, simulate the solvers for all j, giving each fixed solver a fixed share of the simulation time, and return the first answer. All solvers are correct. Since j can be arbitrarily large, the combined algorithm runs in subexponential time and contradicts uniform ETH. This last step adapts the published reduction to the single-algorithm formulation.
equivalences.reverse:
Suppose there were a single subexponential algorithm for 3-SAT. Encode a graph on n vertices using three Boolean variables per vertex, one per color. One clause per vertex requires at least one color. For each edge and each color, a binary clause forbids both endpoints from choosing that color. A satisfying assignment gives a proper coloring by choosing any allowed color at each vertex. Conversely, every proper coloring satisfies the formula.

This is a 3-CNF formula with exactly 3n variables and polynomial length. The assumed 3-SAT algorithm would therefore decide 3-Coloring in subexponential time, contradicting the bound.
equivalences.locator: Daniel Lokshtanov, Dániel Marx, and Saket Saurabh. “Lower bounds based on the Exponential Time Hypothesis.” Bulletin of the EATCS 105, 41–71 (2011). Section 2 (the subexponential-time formulation for 3-CNF-SAT) and Theorem 3.2 (3-Coloring on unrestricted graphs).
equivalences.reverseLocator: Daniel Faber, Adalat Jabrayilov, and Petra Mutzel. “SAT Encoding of Partial Ordering Models for Graph Coloring Problems.” 27th International Conference on Theory and Applications of Satisfiability Testing (SAT 2024), LIPIcs 305, article 12 (2024). Assignment clauses (8a) and (8b), specialized here to three colors.

additionalForwardSources.locator: George B. Mertzios and Paul G. Spirakis. “Algorithms and Almost Tight Results for 3-Colorability of Small Diameter Graphs.” Algorithmica 74, 385–414 (2016). Section 2, definition of ETH and Theorem 2 (diameter 4 and radius 2).

equivalences.forward: The uniform ETH formulation excludes exactly one deterministic 3SAT solver in the displayed subexponential variable-count time family. The polynomial factor is in the complete binary input length on both sides.
equivalences.reverse: The bound is precisely the same exclusion as uniform ETH with the same clauses and measure.
equivalences.locator: Lokshtanov, Marx and Saurabh, Bulletin of the EATCS 105 (2011), §2, ETH in the single-algorithm subexponential convention.

equivalences.forward: Normalize the explicit formula in polynomial time: renumber occurring variables and remove repetitions, leaving polynomial normalized length in n, the number of occurring variables. For each positive integer j, the effective sparsifier with tolerance 1/j branches into at most 2^(n/j) formulas, each with O_j(n) clauses. A single hypothetical solver with a little-o exponent on the target measure therefore gives a correct solver for each j with time 2^(n/j+o(n)) on normalized inputs. Interleave the simulations, giving each fixed j a fixed positive share of the steps, and return the first answer. Every solver is correct. Since j can be chosen arbitrarily large in the time analysis, this is one uniform subexponential variable-count 3SAT algorithm. The proof needs no computable convergence modulus for the target exponent.
equivalences.reverse: If uniform ETH fails, delete unused variables and run its single subexponential solver. A width-three formula with m clauses has at most 3m occurring variables, so the exponent is o(m), with fixed polynomial overhead in the full input.
equivalences.locator: Impagliazzo, Paturi and Zane, JCSS 63 (2001), pp. 519–524, Corollary 1 and its proof (fixed-width decision sparsification), and Lemma 10 (width reduction).

equivalences.forward: Fix the width r≥3. Sparse 3CNF formulas remain admissible r-CNF inputs and have n+m=O_j(n) after sparsification. Normalize the explicit formula in polynomial time: renumber occurring variables and remove repetitions, leaving polynomial normalized length in n, the number of occurring variables. For each positive integer j, the effective sparsifier with tolerance 1/j branches into at most 2^(n/j) formulas, each with O_j(n) clauses. A single hypothetical solver with a little-o exponent on the target measure therefore gives a correct solver for each j with time 2^(n/j+o(n)) on normalized inputs. Interleave the simulations, giving each fixed j a fixed positive share of the steps, and return the first answer. Every solver is correct. Since j can be chosen arbitrarily large in the time analysis, this is one uniform subexponential variable-count 3SAT algorithm. The proof needs no computable convergence modulus for the target exponent.
equivalences.reverse: For each fixed width r≥3, split every long clause with private auxiliary variables into a chain of clauses of width at most three. This preserves satisfiability and introduces O_r(m) variables, where m is the clause count. Together with the original variables, the new count is O_r(n+m). A single variable-count subexponential 3SAT solver gives the claimed total-size clock.
equivalences.locator: Impagliazzo, Paturi and Zane, JCSS 63 (2001), pp. 519–524, Corollary 1 and its proof (fixed-width decision sparsification), and Lemma 10 (width reduction).

equivalences.forward: Uniform ETH excludes a single subexponential variable-count solver for 3SAT. Such a solver for r-SAT, where r≥3 is fixed, would also accept every 3SAT input.
equivalences.reverse: A uniform variable-subexponential solver for 3SAT transfers to every fixed width using the fixed-rate IPZ sparsification and width reduction. After normalizing the occurring variables, each branch has O_j(n) clauses for sparsification tolerance 1/j. Its width-three image has O_j(n) variables, and one call costs 2^o(n). Interleave the resulting correct decision algorithms for all j, using a fixed positive share of time for each fixed j. The first response has a single uniform subexponential worst-case clock, since the exponent contribution n/j for arbitrarily large fixed j is available in the analysis.
